If the side that is opposite to a ${45}^{∘}$ angle in an isosceles right triangle has a length of $\frac{12}{\sqrt{2}},$ what is the length of the hypotenuse?
questions.worked_solution:
The hypotenuse in an isosceles right triangle is equal to $\sqrt{2}$ times the length of a leg.

The legs of an isosceles right triangle are the sides that are opposite the ${45}^{∘}$ angles. So in the given triangle, the legs have length $\frac{12}{\sqrt{2}}.$

Consequently, the hypotenuse has a length of

$$
\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{12}{\sqrt{2}}=\frac{12\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}}=12.
$$

questions.problem: If the hypotenuse of a ${45}^{∘}$-${45}^{∘}$-${90}^{∘}$ triangle has a length of $9$, then what is the length of each leg?
questions.worked_solution:
The hypotenuse in a ${45}^{∘}$-${45}^{∘}$-${90}^{∘}$ triangle is equal to $\sqrt{2}$ times the length of a leg.

Here, we know that the hypotenuse has length $9.$ So, if the length of a leg is $a,$ then we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}9 & =\sqrt{2}\cdot a \\ a & =\frac{9}{\sqrt{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

To remove the square root from the denominator, we can multiply both the numerator and denominator by $\sqrt{2},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{9\cdot \sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{9\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the length of each leg is $\frac{9\sqrt{2}}{2}.$

The perimeter of the triangle above is $16+8\sqrt{2}.$ Find the measure of the hypotenuse.
questions.worked_solution:
Because the triangle is isosceles, the legs must have the same length. Let $a$ be the length of each leg. So, we have

$$
AB=BC=a.
$$

Moreover, because the triangle is a *right* isosceles triangle, the hypotenuse must be equal to $\sqrt{2}$ times the length of a leg. Therefore,

$$
AC=AB\cdot \sqrt{2}=a\sqrt{2}.
$$

Finally, since the perimeter is $p=16+8\sqrt{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}p & =AB+BC+AC \\ 16+8\sqrt{2} & =a+a+a\sqrt{2} \\ 16+8\sqrt{2} & =2a+a\sqrt{2} \\ 8(2+\sqrt{2}) & =a(2+\sqrt{2}) \\ 8\cancel{(2+\sqrt{2})} & =a\cancel{(2+\sqrt{2})} \\ 8 & =a.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the length of each leg is $a=8,$ and the length of the hypotenuse is

$$
AC=a\sqrt{2}=8\sqrt{2}.
$$

questions.problem: Find the perimeter of a square whose diagonal is $\frac{10}{\sqrt{2}}\,mm.$
questions.worked_solution:
A diagram of the given situation is shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14182820/assets/62e30b7b3f72b70df25a16b2d3b48423692892df19c9a7fcf99ba2201bb9ce09.png)

Notice that $△FHG$ is a ${45}^{∘}$-${45}^{∘}$-${90}^{∘}$ triangle since $HG=GF$ and $m∠HGF={90}^{∘}.$

The hypotenuse in an isosceles right triangle is equal to $\sqrt{2}$ times the length of a leg. 

Here, the length of the hypotenuse $\overset{―}{FH}$ is $\frac{10}{\sqrt{2}}\,mm.$ So the length of the leg $\overset{―}{HG}$ can be found by solving the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}FH & =\sqrt{2}\cdot HG \\ \frac{10}{\sqrt{2}} & =\sqrt{2}\cdot HG \\ HG & =\frac{10}{\sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{2}} \\ HG & =\frac{10}{2} \\ HG & =5\,mm\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the perimeter $p$ is given by

$$
p=4\cdot HG=4\cdot 5=20\,mm.
$$

The perimeter of the triangle below is $26+13\sqrt{2}.$ Find the measure of the hypotenuse.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14182820/assets/d194f2c2ce34bd40f5da5dd9e30048a6cc9318a1308c8a7e5d7156cb58a76134.png)

Because the triangle is isosceles, the legs must have the same length. Let $a$ be the length of each leg. So, we have

AB=BC=a.

$$
AC = AB\cdot\sqrt{2} = a\sqrt{2}.
$$

Finally, since the perimeter is $p = 26+13\sqrt{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}p & =AB+BC+AC \\ 26+13\sqrt{2} & =a+a+a\sqrt{2} \\ 26+13\sqrt{2} & =2a+a\sqrt{2} \\ 13(2+\sqrt{2}) & =a(2+\sqrt{2}) \\ 13\cancel{(2+\sqrt{2})} & =a\cancel{(2+\sqrt{2})} \\ 13 & =a.\end{aligned}

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Determining the Length of the Diagonal or Side of a Square Given its Perimeter
canonical_examples.problem: Find the length of the diagonal $\overline{AC}$ of the square $ABCD$ if the perimeter of the square is $p=256\,\mathrm{mm}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Since the perimeter is $p=256\,\textrm{mm},$ the length of a single side is

$$
AB = \dfrac{p}{4} = \dfrac{256}{4} = 64\,\mathrm{mm}.
$$

Now, consider $\triangle{ABC}$, which is an isosceles right triangle since $\angle{ABC} = 90^\circ$ and $AB=BC.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14182820/assets/5bb28a161b88919351ee8e83c2943817f20c124d80fb24c4ceffe29129fbbb07.png)

The hypotenuse in an isosceles right triangle is equal to $\sqrt{2}$ times the length of a leg.

Here, the length of a leg is $AB=64,$ so the length of the hypotenuse is

$$
AC = \sqrt{2}\cdot AB = \sqrt{2}\cdot 64 = 64\sqrt{2}\,\textrm{mm}.
$$

Therefore, the diagonal of the square $ABCD$ has a length of $AC= 64 \sqrt{2} \, \textrm{mm}.$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
In isosceles right triangles such as the one shown below, the angles always measure $45^\circ,$ $45^\circ,$ and $90^\circ.$ 

Consequently, isosceles right triangles are often called **$\boldsymbol{45^\circ}$-$\boldsymbol{45^\circ}$-$\boldsymbol{90^\circ}$ triangles**.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14182820/assets/d32159528abc75f3ed8bcccaedb2765b676fd6cc64164e2f8c81f98eb37f6db4.png)

All $45^\circ$-$45^\circ$-$90^\circ$ triangles share a special property:

*In any ${45^\circ}$-${45^\circ}$-${90^\circ}$ triangle, the length of the hypotenuse is $\sqrt{2}$ times the length of a leg.*

To see why this is, remember that

- in an isosceles triangle, the two legs must have the same length, and

- in a right triangle, the square of the longest side must equal the sum of the squares of the two shorter sides.

So, if an isosceles right triangle has legs of length $a$ and the hypotenuse has length $h,$ then we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{2} & ={a}^{2}+{a}^{2} \\ {h}^{2} & =2{a}^{2} \\ h & =\sqrt{2{a}^{2}} \\ h & =\sqrt{2}\cdot a.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.problem:
Now that we know about $45^\circ$-$45^\circ$-$90^\circ$ triangles, it's straightforward to see that the diagonal of any square is $\sqrt{2}$ times the side length of the square.

To illustrate, consider the square below, where $a$ is the measure of a side and $c$ is the measure of a diagonal.

Since the sides of a square are congruent, $\triangle{ABC}$ is an isosceles right triangle (a $45^{\circ}$-$45^{\circ}$-$90^{\circ}$ triangle). 

So, for the diagonal, we have

$$
